lessons.title: systemd units and systemctl
lessons.goal:
Learn what a systemd unit is, the unit types, and the everyday `systemctl` commands to look at and control services.

Why it matters: systemd is PID 1 on almost every distribution. Every service, mount, timer and socket is a unit, and `systemctl` is how you manage them.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create and remove small `lab-*` services. Use a throwaway machine.
commands: sudo systemctl stop lab-hello lab-app lab-db 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-*.service /usr/local/bin/lab-hello.sh; sudo systemctl daemon-reload

steps.title: Units describe things to manage
steps.text: A **unit** is a text file describing something systemd manages. The type is the file's suffix: `.service` (a daemon), `.socket` (a listening socket that starts a service on demand), `.timer` (schedule), `.mount` (a mount), `.target` (a group, like a runlevel), `.path`, `.slice` (cgroup).

run.cmd: systemctl list-unit-files --no-legend --no-pager | awk '{print $1}' | sed 's/.*\.//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 6
run.output:
274 service
     82 target
     35 socket
     31 timer
     14 mount
      7 scope

steps.title: Look at a service
steps.text: `systemctl cat` prints the unit file(s). `status` summarises state, main PID, the control group and recent log lines.

run.output:
[Unit]
Description=Command Scheduler
After=auditd.service nss-user-lookup.target systemd-user-sessions.service time-sync.target ypbind.service autofs.service
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/sysconfig/crond
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/crond -n $CRONDARGS
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=30s

● crond.service - Command Scheduler
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/crond.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Tue 2026-09-22 15:31:02 GMT; 1 month 16 days ago
   Main PID: 2344 (crond)

steps.title: Ask simple questions with scripts in mind
steps.text: `is-active`, `is-enabled` and `is-failed` print one word and set the exit code, so scripts can use them.

steps.title: Start, stop, restart, reload, enable
steps.text:
- `start` / `stop` act now.
- `restart` stops and starts; `reload` asks the daemon to re-read its configuration (SIGHUP or its own command) without stopping.
- `enable` makes it start at boot (a symlink, see the next lesson); `disable` removes it; `enable --now` does both.

These change the system, so we show them on a service we create in the next lesson.
steps.under: `systemctl` does not start anything itself. It sends a request over D-Bus (or a private socket) to PID 1, which does the work: it forks, sets up the cgroup, namespaces and credentials from the unit file, and then `exec`s the service binary.

steps.title: Targets and dependencies
steps.text: A target is a unit that only groups others. `list-dependencies` shows the tree. `default.target` points to the target reached at boot.

quiz.q: Which suffix marks a systemd timer?
What does `systemctl is-active X` return for a stopped service?
What is the difference between restart and reload?
options: reload asks the daemon to re-read config without stopping
quiz.explain: Reload does not interrupt service if the daemon supports it.

check.scenario: You edited a unit file in `/etc/systemd/system/` and `systemctl restart` still runs the old command. What did you forget?
check.answer: `systemctl daemon-reload`: systemd caches unit files, and a reload makes it read the changed file. (systemd warns: "unit file changed on disk".)

lessons.title: Writing a service: unit file, logs and restart
lessons.goal:
Create a service from scratch, start it, read its logs, watch systemd restart it after a crash, and enable it at boot.

Why it matters: this replaces cron `@reboot` hacks, `nohup` and init scripts. You get supervision, logging and resource control for free.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create and remove small `lab-*` services. Use a throwaway machine.
commands: sudo systemctl stop lab-hello lab-app lab-db 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-*.service /usr/local/bin/lab-hello.sh; sudo systemctl daemon-reload

steps.title: The program
steps.text: A tiny script that logs a line every second. Install it where service binaries belong (`/usr/local/bin`) so SELinux labels it correctly.

code.src:
#!/bin/bash
echo "lab-hello started, pid $$"
n=0
while true; do
    n=$((n + 1))
    echo "tick $n"
    sleep 1
done

steps.title: The unit file
steps.text: Sections: `[Unit]` (description and ordering), `[Service]` (how to run) and `[Install]` (what `enable` does). `Restart=on-failure` makes systemd restart it when it dies abnormally. `User=nobody` drops privileges. Save as `/etc/systemd/system/lab-hello.service`.

code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Lab hello service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/lab-hello.sh
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=1
User=nobody

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

run.cmd: sudo cp lab-hello.service /etc/systemd/system/lab-hello.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload

run.output:
/etc/systemd/system/lab-hello.service:9: Special user nobody configured, this is not safe!
verify exit code: 0

steps.after: `systemd-analyze verify` checks the syntax. Its warning about the user `nobody` is real: sharing one account between services is weak isolation. `DynamicUser=yes` (next lesson) is better.

steps.title: Start it and look
steps.text: `status` shows that it is active, its main PID and the cgroup it runs in.

run.cmd: sudo systemctl start lab-hello; sleep 3; systemctl is-active lab-hello

run.output:
Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/lab-hello.service; disabled; preset: disabled)
     Active: active (running) since Sun 2026-11-08 11:24:35 GMT; 3s ago

run.cmd: systemctl show lab-hello -p User,Restart,Type | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Its output goes to the journal
steps.text: stdout and stderr of the service are captured by journald, tagged with the unit name. `-u` selects the unit and `-o cat` prints only the message.

steps.title: systemd restarts it
steps.text: We kill the main process with SIGKILL, like a crash. systemd notices, waits `RestartSec` and starts it again. The new process has a new PID.

run.cmd: old=$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value lab-hello); sudo kill -9 $old; sleep 3; new=$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value lab-hello); [ "$new" != "$old" ] && [ "$new" -gt 0 ] && echo 'restarted with a new PID'
journalctl -u lab-hello -o cat --no-pager | grep -E 'Main process exited|Scheduled restart|Failed with result' | sed -E 's/[0-9]{3,}/<n>/g'
run.output:
lab-hello.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
lab-hello.service: Failed with result 'signal'.
lab-hello.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.
lab-hello.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
lab-hello.service: Failed with result 'signal'.
lab-hello.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.

steps.title: Enable at boot, then clean up
steps.text: `enable` creates a symlink from the target's `.wants` directory to the unit file, as the `[Install]` section says. That is all that "enabled" means.

run.cmd: sudo systemctl enable lab-hello 2>&1 | sed 's/ -> .*//'; systemctl is-enabled lab-hello
sudo systemctl disable --now lab-hello 2>&1 | sed 's/ -> .*//'; sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/lab-hello.service /usr/local/bin/lab-hello.sh; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl is-active lab-hello

steps.under: At boot, systemd starts `multi-user.target`, which **Wants** everything in `multi-user.target.wants/`. The symlink is the only difference between enabled and disabled. `Type=simple` (the default) means the process started by `ExecStart` is the service. Old-style daemons that fork into the background need `Type=forking` and a `PIDFile=`.

options: Restarts the service after an abnormal exit
quiz.explain: Crashes, non-zero exit, signals and timeouts count as failure.

options: Creates the symlink so the service starts at boot

quiz.q: Where should local unit files be placed?
Which command shows a unit's log lines?

check.scenario: A Python app is started by systemd as `ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 app.py` and always shows `inactive (dead)` right after start, though the script works by hand. What do you check?
check.answer: `journalctl -u NAME -b` for the error, then: a relative path in `ExecStart` (systemd needs absolute paths) or `WorkingDirectory=`; missing environment variables (set `Environment=` or `EnvironmentFile=`); the `User=` cannot read the files; SELinux denial (`ausearch -m avc -ts recent`); or the script forks and exits, which needs `Type=forking` or fixing the script to stay in the foreground.

lessons.title: Dependencies, ordering and sandboxing
lessons.goal:
Learn the difference between "needs" and "starts after" in systemd, and use the sandboxing options that make a service safer.

Why it matters: wrong dependencies cause race conditions at boot and cascading stops. Sandboxing limits the damage when a service is compromised.

setup.note: Steps with sudo create and remove small `lab-*` services. Use a throwaway machine.
commands: sudo systemctl stop lab-hello lab-app lab-db 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/lab-*.service /usr/local/bin/lab-hello.sh; sudo systemctl daemon-reload

steps.title: Two units: the database
steps.text: `lab-db` is a stand-in database that prints a line and sleeps.

code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Lab database

[Service]
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo db-up; exec sleep 300'

steps.title: The application unit
steps.text: Two separate ideas: `Requires=` is a **dependency** (pull the other unit in; stop me if it stops). `After=` is **ordering** (start me later). They are independent, so you normally write both.

code.src:
[Unit]
Description=Lab application
Requires=lab-db.service
After=lab-db.service

[Service]
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'echo app-up; exec sleep 300'

run.cmd: sudo cp lab-db.service lab-app.service /etc/systemd/system/; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; cat lab-app.service | sed -n '3,4p'

steps.title: Starting the app pulls in the database
steps.text: We start only `lab-app`. systemd starts `lab-db` first because of `Requires` and `After`.

run.cmd: sudo systemctl start lab-app; sleep 1; systemctl is-active lab-db lab-app | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Stopping the database stops the app
steps.text: `Requires` propagates stops. With `Wants=` (a weaker dependency) the app would keep running.

run.cmd: sudo systemctl stop lab-db; sleep 1; systemctl is-active lab-app lab-db | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.under: systemd builds a **transaction** from the requested unit, its dependencies and the ordering edges, checks for cycles, and then runs the jobs in parallel where ordering allows. Ordering and dependency are separate graphs: ordering only matters between units that are both in the transaction.

steps.title: Sandbox a service
steps.text: Options such as `ProtectSystem=strict` (the file system is read-only for the service), `PrivateTmp=yes` (its own empty `/tmp`) and `NoNewPrivileges=yes` apply namespaces and restrictions. `systemd-run` runs a command as a transient unit with such options.

run.output:
touch: cannot touch '/usr/lab-test': Read-only file system
exit=1

run.cmd: touch /tmp/lab/visible.txt; sudo systemd-run --pipe --wait --collect -q -p PrivateTmp=yes sh -c 'ls /tmp | wc -l'; ls /tmp | wc -l | awk '{print "host /tmp entries (more than 0):", ($1 > 0)}'

steps.title: Score a unit
steps.text: `systemd-analyze security` rates a unit's exposure from 0 (very safe) to 10 (UNSAFE) based on how many protections it uses. Compare the plain unit with a hardened one.

run.cmd: sudo systemd-analyze security lab-app --no-pager | tail -n 1 | sed 's/^→ //' | cut -c1-70
run.output: Overall exposure level for lab-app.service: 9.6 UNSAFE 😨

run.cmd:
sudo sed -i '/^\[Service\]/a ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
DynamicUser=yes' /etc/systemd/system/lab-app.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; sudo systemd-analyze security lab-app --no-pager | tail -n 1 | sed 's/^→ //' | cut -c1-70
run.output: Overall exposure level for lab-app.service: 7.5 EXPOSED 🙁

run.cmd: sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/lab-app.service /etc/systemd/system/lab-db.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload; echo cleaned

options: A dependency: the other unit is started and a failure or stop propagates
Orders the start only if both are being started
quiz.explain: It does not pull lab-db in.

options: A private empty /tmp for the service
quiz.explain: The service cannot see or interfere with other processes' temp files.

quiz.q: Which command rates a unit's sandboxing?

check.scenario: A nightly import job runs as root via a unit and parses files uploaded by customers. How do you reduce the damage of an exploit in the parser?
check.answer: Run it as an unprivileged user (`User=` or `DynamicUser=yes`), `ProtectSystem=strict` with `ReadWritePaths=` only for its data directory, `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=` empty, `SystemCallFilter=@system-service`, `RestrictAddressFamilies=`, and measure with `systemd-analyze security`.

interview.a: A configuration file describing something systemd manages: service, socket, timer, mount, target, path, slice. See [the lesson](#/lesson/25/units-and-systemctl).

interview.q: What do the sections of a service unit do?
interview.a: [Unit] describes and orders it, [Service] says how to run it, [Install] says which target wants it when enabled. See [writing a service](#/lesson/25/write-a-service).
Creates a symlink in the target's .wants directory, as the [Install] section says. Starting at boot follows from that link.

interview.q: Difference between Requires, Wants and After?
interview.a: Requires and Wants are dependencies (hard and soft); After/Before is ordering. They are independent. See [dependencies](#/lesson/25/dependencies-and-sandboxing).

interview.q: How does systemd restart a crashed service?
interview.a: With `Restart=` (on-failure, always...) and `RestartSec=`. Limits (`StartLimitBurst`) stop endless loops.

interview.q: How can you reduce the attack surface of a service?
interview.a: Run unprivileged and use sandbox options: ProtectSystem, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, NoNewPrivileges, capability and syscall filters; check with systemd-analyze security.

glossary.def: A systemd configuration object: service, timer, socket, mount, target...
A unit that describes a process to start and supervise.
A unit that groups other units to define a system state.
Makes systemd re-read unit files from disk.
Hard dependency: the other unit is started and stops propagate.
Restricting a service with namespaces and filters (ProtectSystem, PrivateTmp, ...).
